doc.title: Harold Ousley interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: Coming to New York in 1957 with Duke Jenkins and the Turf, Beefsteak Charlie's, Flanders
summary: Ousley describes how he got to New York through Duke Jenkins's band and Big Shows, and the Broadway musicians' hangouts and hotel.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: It seems like New York was a magnet for almost all musicians. And you went there eventually?

Yeah. Well musicians who had been in New York would come back to Chicago and tell us about all the wonderful things happening in New York, who they saw, and at this particular time, 52nd Street was the street that was going as well as Minton’s uptown. And these were the musicians we used to listen to on the records, so we were always, you know, open ears and say well we’ve got to go to New York. And I finally got the opportunity through a friend of mine, a trumpet player who moved to Cleveland. And there was a band leader, he was a bass player named Duke Jenkins, had a band there and he used to, I think it was the Rose Room he used to play in. But he was well known in Cleveland. And he was getting ready to come to New York so he was forming a bigger band, a ten piece band. And they were having, during this time they had what they called the Big, Big Shows. That was, you saw they had more than one artist on the show. Because prior to that time when you’d go to a concert you’d just see one artist. You know Roy Hamilton was one of the stars, and Billy Williams’ quartet. Because they had been on “Toast of the Town” and so they were the stars. And then Jerry Lee Lewis had “Great Balls of Fire,” a hit out there. So these were the artists on the show. And we played in Rhode Island and we played in Hartford, Connecticut, and did we play New York? We played in the surrounding area, but this gave me the opportunity to come here to New York. So that’s how I got here. And the first place I stayed was at the hotel where Minton’s is. And I could hear the music upstairs, so that was heaven. I went down, the first thing I did was went downstairs to hear the music. Because I had been hearing about Minton’s. And the next day I went downtown because somebody had told me about a hotel down there that all the musicians lived in, and also, at that time on Broadway everybody used to frequent a couple of — there was a place called The Turf, and it was right next store to Lyndon’s, between 49th and 50th on Broadway. So everybody would come in there and you’d meet, because you would run into people and you’d get gigs. Get record dates or what they called demo dates. They used to have demo dates that didn’t © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

pay as much as record dates, but a lot of times you might be able to do five or six demo dates in a day so that was, you know, good money. So you would go in from one bar to another and see who you could find. It was like a networking, like here you just went around to see, you know, no telling who you might run into. But everybody used to go to The Turf or either there was Beefsteak Charlie’s. Now Beefsteak Charlie’s was the place where Milt Hinton and a lot of the musicians who were playing a lot of the better gigs, you know at Jim and Andy’s, who were on the record dates. So if you wanted to get into that, you know to meet someone, then you would go there. And at Beefsteak Charlie’s, Hawk — I used to see Coleman Hawkins, a lot of musicians, like a lot of the older musicians as well as the younger musicians would come in there, because you’d see these musicians and then you’d get gigs and demos and whatever was happening. But it was always a good place, and Papa Jo would be there. And so you know that was a great time during this time. And I lived at — the hotel they had told me about was The Flanders. And that was, they had two entrances, between 48th Street, they had a 48th Street entrance, and 47th Street. And all the musicians, whoever’s band you were in would stay there because the rent was economical. At that time I think you could get a room for $15, room and bath for $18. And plus you were right there at Times Square, the automat was open and you could go to the automat and you could get a meal for 50 cents, a dollar, a dollar and a quarter. And then you could sit up front in the window and you’re looking out on Broadway. And then you’d go three blocks up and that’s where The Turf was. And you’d go to 51st Street around to where Beefsteak Charlie’s was, and you’d go down to 52nd Street, there’s where Jim and Andy’s was. So people would be going back and forth. And then they had, like in the Brill Building and a couple of other buildings centered in that area, they would have the little small studios. That’s where you would go and do the demos. And the purpose of the demo was say for an artist who might not have had money to go in the studio, but he could go and do a demo date, and like if he had an agent, the agent would get a demo done on him. And they’d get the musician, and everybody saving money, but at the same time they’re making money but the artist gets a chance maybe to take his demo now to the record label. So it was a lot of activity like that going on.
